tagline: Two lanes from western buttes to the Sandhills and Niobrara bridges
intro: The Bridges to Buttes Byway follows US 20 for 197 miles between the Wyoming border and Valentine. It is one of Nebraska’s designated scenic byways, a two-lane drive through bluffs, escarpments and the Sandhills. The Nebraska Tourism Commission emphasizes the change from rolling Sandhills in the east to prairie and pine-studded buttes toward the west.

The highway acquired a single identity in stages. Several state route numbers crossed northern Nebraska in 1922; these were consolidated as N-1 before becoming US 20 in 1926. The alignment changed too. West of Fort Robinson, the old highway followed what is now Smiley Canyon Scenic Drive, a winding road north of the present route. A year-long campaign by Chadron residents brought another road name: in 2010, Governor Dave Heineman approved honoring Crazy Horse on US 20 between Hay Springs and Fort Robinson.

Driving east from the Wyoming line, rolling plains lead to Harrison, then bluffs and the Red Cloud Buttes at Fort Robinson. Beyond Crawford and Chadron, the road climbs 400 feet through part of the Pine Ridge Escarpment toward Hay Springs. Rushville and Gordon give way to the Sandhills; farther east, US 20 follows Minnechaduza Creek toward Valentine and the byway’s end.

moments.title: Fort Robinson
moments.text: Fort Robinson began as a military camp associated with the Red Cloud Agency. Crazy Horse surrendered here with 1,100 followers in May 1877. That September, Private William Gentles bayoneted him outside the guardhouse during an attempt to imprison him; he died in the adjutant’s office. In January 1879, Northern Cheyenne prisoners broke out after the military withheld food, water and firewood to force their return to Indian Territory. U.S. soldiers pursued them, killing men, women and children. A plaque marks the site of Crazy Horse’s death. The former Army post is now part of Fort Robinson State Park, west of Crawford on US 20.

moments.title: Toadstool Geologic Park
moments.text: Toadstool Geologic Park takes its name from rock formations shaped like toadstools. North of Crawford in the Oglala National Grassland, it combines a badlands landscape with a reconstructed sod house. A one-mile loop trail passes fossils. Remains of large prehistoric animals, including entelodonts and hyaenodons, have been found here. A separate three-mile Bison Trail leads toward Hudson-Meng Bison Kill, crossing Whitehead Creek and the ravine it forms between the park and the interpretive center.
moments.notice: The toadstool-shaped rock formations give the park its name.

moments.title: Bryan Bridge
moments.text: Bryan Bridge was built in 1932 to carry US 20 over the Niobrara near Valentine. The bridge bears the name of Charles W. Bryan, Nebraska’s governor when it was built. Its pin-connected cantilever arch was an engineering choice with an eye to the landscape. Designer Josef Sorkin told the National Register nominator that the design blended into its surroundings and was economical for the site. The American Institute of Steel Construction selected it as the year’s most beautiful steel bridge in the category costing less than $250,000. US 20 now crosses the river north of the old bridge.
